title: The IMF’s boost to China’s currency is costing the world, ten years later
gist: Ten years after the IMF admitted the renminbi to the SDR basket on the assumption Beijing would liberalize, China's capital account is little changed: the renminbi is only 2 percent of global reserves, 3.8 percent of international payments, and the IMF estimates it is undervalued by 17.3 to 25.3 percent. The author argues this has seeded a parallel monetary system rather than internationalization, and that in a future crisis a US unable or unwilling to supply dollar liquidity would hand Beijing a renminbi chokepoint comparable to its critical minerals leverage.

themes.theme: The 2016 SDR decision and what it assumed

insights.claim: The IMF admitted the renminbi to the SDR basket while China operated a monetary system fundamentally at odds with the open regimes underpinning the dollar, euro, pound, and yen, resting the decision on an assumption that Beijing would eventually loosen its grip on the currency.
insights.so_what: The entire legitimacy of renminbi reserve status rests on a liberalization that has not happened — a standing argument for discounting official renminbi reserve statistics.
insights.locator: The IMF’s decision to add the renminbi to the SDR basket
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: In 2016 the renminbi was no more important in government reserves than the Canadian and Australian dollars and had only a minor presence among tradable currencies, so the SDR decision was met with considerable skepticism at the time.
insights.so_what: Establishes that the inclusion was political and prospective rather than merited by usage — the baseline against which ten years of non-progress is judged.
insights.locator: Keeping a lid on
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: What was publicly presented as a sweeping endorsement of China's policies was in fact a narrow technical judgment about whether the renminbi could be drawn on to fund IMF crisis loans and obtained by borrowing countries to repay them.
insights.so_what: The 'freely usable' designation carries far less analytical weight than markets have assumed — a reason to treat SDR membership as a poor proxy for currency openness.
insights.quote: What was presented to the public as a sweeping endorsement of China’s policies was, in fact, a much narrower technical judgment.
insights.locator: Debatable definitions
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: The other SDR currencies already had open capital accounts and were widely traded in financial markets when they were included, making China the sole exception to the basket's implicit standard.
insights.so_what: The same 'freely usable' test applied to a structurally different currency is the definitional loophole that any future review would need to close.
insights.locator: But unlike China’s, those currencies already had open capital accounts
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

themes.theme: Ten years of non-adoption, in numbers

insights.claim: At the end of 2024 only 3.8 percent of all international payments were in renminbi, a broader category than trade finance and settlement.
insights.so_what: The payments share is the cleanest rebuttal to de-dollarization narratives built on trade-settlement headlines.
insights.locator: At the end of 2024, only 3.8 percent
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: As of July the renminbi was only the sixth-largest reserve holding at 2 percent of all reserves, trailing not just the other four SDR currencies but also the Canadian dollar, which is not in the SDR basket, and that share has barely budged since 2016.
insights.so_what: Reserve share is the author's stated true measure of a currency's global standing, and it shows zero progress in a decade — a strong argument against imminent dollar displacement.
insights.quote: At 2 percent of all reserves, it trails not only the other four SDR currencies, but also the Canadian dollar, which is not in the SDR basket.
insights.locator: And in terms of government foreign-exchange reserves
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: The value of yuan bonds and loans issued in China and abroad by foreign governments and companies tripled in the five years through March 2026 to a record of nearly $150 billion, still a fraction of the $14 trillion of dollar credit outstanding beyond US borders at year-end 2025.
insights.so_what: A roughly 100-to-1 ratio in offshore credit is the scale gap that any renminbi funding alternative would have to close — dollar funding dominance is not close to being challenged.
insights.locator: The fragmentation threat
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Over-the-counter trading of the renminbi rose to nearly 9 percent of all currency trades last year while its share of official reserves remained largely unchanged, showing trading volume and reserve status have decoupled.
insights.so_what: Rising turnover without rising reserve share means renminbi trading growth is transactional, not a store-of-value shift — do not read FX volume as reserve diversification.
insights.locator: While over-the-counter trading of the renminbi rose
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: In 2024 the renminbi accounted for 27 percent of China's trade in goods and 32 percent of its trade in services, a dramatic rise since 2016 even as capital account controls remained little changed.
insights.so_what: Trade-settlement penetration is the one metric that has genuinely moved — the bull case for the renminbi lives here, not in reserves.
insights.locator: Since then, China has become the world’s largest exporter
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Under Xi Jinping, China has used capital and currency controls to keep domestic resources captive for financing investment priorities like advanced technology and to limit exposure to the dollar-based economy, thereby reducing vulnerability to economic sanctions.
insights.so_what: Sanctions-proofing is the strategic rationale for non-liberalization, which means the controls will not be relaxed for market-access reasons.
insights.locator: Under its leader Xi Jinping, China has used these restrictions
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Alicia Garcia Herrero, chief Asia-Pacific economist at Natixis, argues that what China is pursuing looks less like currency internationalization than the construction of an alternative monetary system for the renminbi's cross-border use.
insights.so_what: Reframes renminbi policy from convergence to parallel-system building — different implications for payments infrastructure, settlement rails, and sanctions design.
insights.quote: looks less like the internationalization of a currency but more like the construction of an alternative monetary system for the renminbi’s cross-border use
insights.locator: In a note last month, Alicia Garcia Herrero
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Bastian von Beschwitz, chief of global financial markets at the US Federal Reserve Board, wrote in 2024 that Beijing's exchange rate management and capital controls limit the renminbi's widespread use to the point that it remains a niche currency internationally.
insights.so_what: A Fed staff judgment that the renminbi is 'niche' is the official-sector view underpinning continued dollar-centric reserve management.
insights.locator: Bastian von Beschwitz, chief of global financial markets
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Every Chinese reform undertaken in the name of internationalization — foreign access to onshore stock and bond markets, outbound flows mostly via Hong Kong, offshore renminbi deposits, expanded yuan lending, offshore yuan bond issuance, and cross-border payments systems — has remained firmly under Beijing's control.
insights.so_what: Access can be withdrawn as easily as it was granted, which is the embedded political risk in any onshore China allocation.
insights.locator: Limited progress
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: The IMF itself has acknowledged that impediments remain to widespread renminbi adoption, that offshore RMB markets lack depth and liquidity, and that a shortage of globally accessible safe RMB assets hinders the currency's store-of-value function.
insights.so_what: The absence of a deep safe-asset market is the binding technical constraint on reserve adoption — watch onshore government bond accessibility as the real leading indicator.
insights.quote: offshore RMB markets lack depth and liquidity, while a shortage of globally accessible safe RMB assets hinders the RMB’s function as a store of value
insights.locator: In its most recent review of the Chinese economy
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

themes.theme: Undervaluation, the export surge, and fragmentation risk

insights.claim: The IMF recently estimated the renminbi is undervalued by between 17.3 percent and 25.3 percent, and that undervaluation has helped drive China's export surge.
insights.so_what: An official IMF undervaluation range of up to 25 percent is direct ammunition for tariff and currency-manipulation actions against China.
insights.locator: The IMF recently estimated that the currency was undervalued
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: The export surge enabled by a managed renminbi is a crucial source of growth for a Chinese economy facing a real estate collapse, an investment slowdown, and plummeting consumer confidence.
insights.so_what: Beijing cannot allow renminbi appreciation while domestic demand is broken — currency liberalization is structurally off the table until the property drag clears.
insights.locator: That has, in turn, helped drive China’s massive export surge
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: China's renminbi policy is not merely a domestic choice but a contributing factor in the ongoing process of global economic fragmentation.
insights.so_what: Ties currency policy directly to the trade-bloc dynamic — a reason to expect continued escalation in tariff and capital measures targeting China.
insights.quote: China’s approach to the renminbi is therefore not just a domestic policy choice, but a contributing factor in the ongoing process of global economic fragmentation.
insights.locator: That has, in turn, helped drive China’s massive export surge
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: If a future US government were unable or unwilling to provide the dollar liquidity needed in a crisis, a surge in demand for renminbi resources could give Beijing a new chokepoint to exploit, just as it has done with critical minerals, with countries in financial distress paying a political or economic price for access.
insights.so_what: The non-obvious tail risk: renminbi weaponization becomes plausible only conditional on a US swap-line failure — a scenario to price rather than a base case.
insights.quote: a surge in demand for renminbi resources could give Beijing a new chokepoint to exploit, just as it has done with critical minerals
insights.locator: The fragmentation threat
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: There would likely be little support for removing the renminbi from the SDR basket even given how Beijing has gamed the system, particularly at a time of growing economic uncertainty.
insights.so_what: Rules out the cleanest corrective action, so expect rhetorical pressure rather than institutional change — no near-term catalyst for repricing.
insights.locator: Ramping up the pressure
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: The IMF reassesses SDR currency weightings every five years with the next review expected to be completed by July 2027, giving a concrete date to push China toward opening its capital account.
insights.so_what: July 2027 is the calendarable event risk for renminbi reserve-status headlines.
insights.locator: The IMF reassesses the currency weightings in the basket
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: The IMF should strengthen the language in its Articles of Agreement on the requirements for a 'freely usable' currency, and the G7, which the US chairs next year, should reinforce those calls.
insights.so_what: A G7 chaired by Washington is the venue where renminbi convertibility pressure would surface — watch next year's agenda for it.
insights.locator: The IMF should also strengthen the language
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Xi Jinping is on one of his busiest foreign trips in years, including a summit with President Donald Trump this month, as he seeks to signal China's commitment to the global order.
insights.so_what: Gives a near-term window where a Chinese gesture on capital account or currency policy would be most likely, if one comes at all.
insights.locator: Xi is currently on one of his busiest trips abroad
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
